# Non-Congruence Veech Groups of Translation Surfaces

## Main Result

The central contribution of this article establishes a significant result concerning the algebraic structure of Veech groups. Specifically, we prove that for every genus $g > 1$, there exists a translation surface whose Veech group is a non-congruence subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This result is notable because it demonstrates that non-congruence subgroups arise naturally within the geometry of translation surfaces, extending our understanding of the possible arithmetic properties these groups can exhibit.

## Method of Construction

To prove this result, we rely on a particularly tractable class of translation surfaces known as origamis, or equivalently, square-tiled surfaces. These objects are constructed by gluing together finitely many unit squares according to prescribed combinatorial rules, making them especially amenable to explicit computation. Their concrete nature allows us to analyze their Veech groups directly, providing the necessary examples that establish the main theorem.

## Structure of the Article

### Part One: Foundations and Initial Examples

The first part of the article lays the theoretical groundwork by introducing the foundational concepts underlying our investigation. We begin with a treatment of translation surfaces, followed by a detailed discussion of origamis and their combinatorial description. We then introduce Veech groups, which encode the affine symmetries of a translation surface, and Teichmüller curves, which arise as the projections of the orbits of these surfaces under the action of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$.

Building on this framework, we present our first concrete results. We demonstrate that the Veech groups of two specific genus $2$ origamis are non-congruence subgroups. These initial examples serve both to illustrate the relevant techniques and to establish the base cases from which more general results can be developed.

### Part Two: A General Construction Technique

The second part of the article develops the machinery required to prove the main result in full generality. Here, we introduce a technique for generating sequences of origamis whose associated Veech groups form a decreasing chain. This construction is essential to our argument, as it allows us to propagate the non-congruence property to surfaces of arbitrarily high genus. By carefully controlling the behavior of the Veech groups along these sequences, we obtain, for each genus $g > 1$, a translation surface realizing the desired non-congruence property.

# Translation Surfaces, Origamis, and Non-Congruence Veech Groups

## Background and Motivation

Translation surfaces occupy a central place in the study of dynamical systems, Teichmüller theory, and the geometry of moduli spaces. A translation surface is obtained by taking a finite collection of polygons in the plane and gluing their edges in parallel pairs by translations, producing a closed surface equipped with a flat metric that has finitely many cone-type singularities. The genus $g$ of the resulting surface measures its topological complexity, and surfaces with $g > 1$ exhibit particularly rich geometric and dynamical behavior.

Associated to every translation surface is its **Veech group**, a subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ (or more generally $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$) consisting of the linear parts of the affine automorphisms of the surface. The Veech group encodes the symmetries of the surface and governs the behavior of geodesic flow, making its determination a fundamental problem. Understanding which subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ can appear as Veech groups is a longstanding question that connects flat geometry to arithmetic.

## The Role of Origamis

To make these questions tractable, one restricts attention to **origamis**, also called square-tiled surfaces. An origami is a translation surface built by gluing finitely many unit squares along their edges, so that right edges are identified with left edges and top edges with bottom edges. Combinatorially, an origami is described by a pair of permutations recording the horizontal and vertical gluings, which makes these surfaces amenable to explicit computation.

Origamis are precisely the translation surfaces that arise as coverings of the standard torus $\mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$ branched over a single point. Because of this covering structure, their Veech groups are always **finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$**. This finiteness makes origamis an ideal testing ground for studying which subgroups actually occur, since the entire theory becomes accessible through combinatorics and group theory rather than requiring transcendental analytic methods.

## A Technique for Decreasing Veech Groups

The central methodological contribution is a technique that produces **sequences of origamis whose Veech groups form a decreasing chain**. Starting from a given origami, one constructs successive coverings or modifications in a controlled way, so that each new surface in the sequence has a Veech group contained in that of its predecessor. By carefully tracking how the combinatorial data transforms under these operations, one gains precise control over the index of the Veech group and over its algebraic structure.

This descending construction is powerful because it allows one to engineer surfaces whose Veech groups have prescribed properties. In particular, by pushing the construction far enough, one can force the Veech group to escape the class of congruence subgroups, which are the subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ defined by congruence conditions modulo some integer $N$.

## The Main Result

The principal theorem states that **for every genus $g > 1$, there exists a translation surface whose Veech group is a non-congruence subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$**. 

This result is significant for several reasons. First, it settles the question of existence uniformly: rather than exhibiting isolated examples in specific genera, it demonstrates that non-congruence Veech groups appear systematically throughout all higher genera. Second, it highlights a genuine difference between the arithmetic of Veech groups and the classical theory of congruence subgroups, showing that the geometric constraints imposed by translation surface structure do not restrict Veech groups to the congruence world.

The distinction between congruence and non-congruence subgroups is subtle and important. Congruence subgroups are comparatively well understood and enjoy strong arithmetic properties, whereas non-congruence subgroups are far more numerous and much harder to analyze. The demonstration that Veech groups can be non-congruence in every higher genus therefore reveals that the family of translation surfaces reaches into this less tractable and more mysterious region of subgroup space.

## Significance and Conclusion

By combining the combinatorial accessibility of origamis with a systematic method for producing descending sequences of Veech groups, this work provides both a flexible tool and a definitive structural result. The technique itself is of independent interest, as it may be applied to construct surfaces with other prescribed properties. Meanwhile, the main theorem enriches our understanding of the interplay between flat geometry, dynamics, and arithmetic, confirming that non-congruence phenomena are an unavoidable and pervasive feature of translation surfaces of higher genus.

# Veech Groups and Teichmüller Theory

## Introduction

The interplay between **Veech groups** and **Teichmüller theory** represents one of the most fascinating areas of modern geometry and dynamical systems. Named after mathematician William A. Veech, whose pioneering work in the 1980s and 1990s reshaped our understanding of translation surfaces, these concepts bridge several branches of mathematics, including complex analysis, dynamical systems, and the study of moduli spaces.

## Teichmüller Theory: The Foundation

Teichmüller theory, developed by Oswald Teichmüller in the 1930s, studies the space of complex structures on a given surface. The **Teichmüller space** of a surface parametrizes all possible ways to endow that surface with a conformal or hyperbolic structure, up to isotopy. This space carries a natural metric—the Teichmüller metric—which measures the minimal distortion required to deform one complex structure into another.

The genius of this framework lies in its ability to capture geometric flexibility in a rigorous analytical setting. Teichmüller geodesics, the shortest paths in this metric, correspond to families of surfaces undergoing controlled stretching and shrinking in prescribed directions.

## The Veech Group

A **Veech group** arises when we consider a **translation surface**—a surface built by gluing polygons along parallel sides via translations. The Veech group is the group of affine symmetries of such a surface, specifically the derivatives of orientation-preserving affine automorphisms. These derivatives form a subgroup of $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$.

Veech's celebrated **dichotomy** demonstrated that when this group is a lattice (a so-called **Veech surface** or **lattice surface**), the dynamics of the associated flow exhibit remarkable rigidity. In every direction, the flow is either:

- **Completely periodic**, decomposing the surface into cylinders, or
- **Uniquely ergodic**, distributing trajectories uniformly.

This clean dichotomy stands in stark contrast to the complicated behavior seen in general dynamical systems.

## The Connection

The bridge between these ideas is profound. The action of $SL(2, \mathbb{R})$ on the moduli space of translation surfaces corresponds precisely to the Teichmüller geodesic flow. Orbits of this action encode the deformation of flat structures, and the stabilizer of a translation surface under this action is exactly its Veech group.

When the Veech group is a lattice, the corresponding orbit in moduli space is closed, producing a **Teichmüller curve**—an isometrically immersed algebraic curve of great arithmetic and geometric significance.

## Conclusion

The synthesis of Veech's insights with classical Teichmüller theory has opened rich avenues of research, influencing work on billiards in polygons, interval exchange transformations, and the celebrated results of Eskin, Mirzakhani, and Mohammadi on orbit closures. Together, these ideas illuminate the deep unity underlying dynamics, geometry, and arithmetic.

# Abstract

Origamis (also known as square-tiled surfaces) provide a powerful combinatorial framework for constructing explicit examples of translation surfaces whose Veech groups exhibit subtle arithmetic properties. In this work, we exploit the correspondence between origamis and finite-index subgroups of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ to systematically produce examples of **non-congruence Veech groups** in genus 2 and higher.

An origami is defined by gluing finitely many unit squares along their edges via translations, encoded by a pair of permutations $(\sigma_h, \sigma_v)$ generating a transitive subgroup of the symmetric group. The associated Veech group—the stabilizer of the origami under the $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ action—is always a finite-index subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. A central question concerns whether such subgroups are **congruence** (containing a principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$) or not.

We develop explicit combinatorial and computational criteria to determine the congruence level of the Veech groups arising from families of origamis. Beginning in genus 2, where the stratum structure and the action of the affine group are well understood, we construct origamis whose Veech groups fail the congruence property, verified via the Wohlfahrt level and explicit generators. We then extend these constructions to higher genus by suitable coverings and combinatorial surgery, showing that non-congruence phenomena are not exceptional but persist and proliferate as the genus grows.

Our results illustrate that, in contrast to the classical setting of arithmetic Fuchsian groups, Veech groups of origamis form a rich source of non-congruence subgroups. These examples shed light on the arithmetic and geometric complexity of the $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits of square-tiled surfaces, and provide concrete testing grounds for questions relating Teichmüller dynamics, modular forms, and the structure of finite-index subgroups of the modular group.
